## Statement

Assume AC. For $d\ge1$, let $\gamma_d$ be standard Gaussian measure on $\mathbb R^d$,
let $A\subseteq\mathbb R^d$ be Borel, and let
$A+rB_2^d=\{a+ru:a\in A,\ |u|\le1\}$. Then for every $r\ge0$,
$$\gamma_{d,*}(A+rB_2^d)\ge \Phi\!\left(\Phi^{-1}(\gamma_d(A))+r\right),$$
where $\gamma_{d,*}(S)=\sup\{\gamma_d(K):K\subseteq S,\ K\text{ compact}\}$ is Gaussian inner measure, and $\Phi^{-1}(0)=-\infty$, $\Phi^{-1}(1)=+\infty$.


## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** AC, $d\ge1$, standard Gaussian measure $\gamma_d$, a Borel set $A$, and $r\ge0$.

[F1] The Gaussian density is $(2\pi)^{-d/2}e^{-|x|^2/2}$; independent standard Gaussian vectors form a joint Gaussian vector, and orthogonal linear combinations have their stated Gaussian laws. The scalar CDF $\Phi$ is continuous and strictly increasing onto $(0,1)$. [[def-standard-normal-and-normal-laws]], [[def-multivariate-normal-law]], [[lem-finite-independent-gaussian-vectors-form-joint-multivariate-normal]], [[lem-standard-normal-cdf-is-continuous-and-strictly-increasing]].

[F2] Differentiation under the integral follows from an integrable majorant, dominated convergence passes dominated limits, and Fubini applies to absolutely integrable functions. [[thm-differentiation-under-the-integral-sign]], [[thm-dominated-convergence]], [[thm-fubini-theorem-for-l-one-on-sigma-finite-product-spaces]].

[F3] Integration by parts and the fundamental theorem apply on one-dimensional absolutely continuous slices. AC implies their DC and Countable Choice assumptions. [[thm-integration-by-parts-for-absolutely-continuous-functions]], [[thm-fundamental-theorem-of-calculus-for-absolutely-continuous-functions]], [[thm-choice-implies-dependent-implies-countable-choice]], [[def-axiom-of-choice]].

[F4] Borel probabilities on Polish spaces are inner regular. [[thm-borel-probability-measures-on-polish-spaces-are-inner-regular]].

[F5] A unit-mass smooth bump gives the scaled convolution family. One may choose it nonnegative and supported in the unit ball by normalizing $\exp(-1/(1-|x|^2))\mathbf1_{\{|x|<1\}}$. [[def-mollifier-family-generated-by-a-unit-mass-smooth-bump]].

[F6] Under Countable Choice, the nonnegative Lebesgue change-of-variables theorem applies to Euclidean dilations and orthogonal maps; hence a ball of radius $R$ has volume $v_dR^d$ with finite $v_d$ bounded by the volume of the containing cube. [[thm-c-one-change-of-variables-for-nonnegative-lebesgue-measurable-functions]].

## Proof

**Given:** The objects and assumptions above. Write $\varphi=\Phi'$ and $I=\varphi\circ\Phi^{-1}$ on $(0,1)$, with $I(0)=I(1)=0$.

1.1 Differentiating $\varphi'=-x\varphi$ and $(\Phi^{-1})'=1/I$ gives $I'=-\Phi^{-1}$ and $II''=-1$. The function $I$ is continuous on $[0,1]$, positive on $(0,1)$ and bounded by $(2\pi)^{-1/2}$. First take a smooth $f$ valued in $[\eta,1-\eta]$, $0<\eta<1/2$, with all derivatives bounded. Define $P_tf(x)=\int f(e^{-t}x+\sqrt{1-e^{-2t}}y)\gamma_d(dy)$ and $u_t=P_tf$. Gaussian integration by parts in $y$ gives $\partial_tu_t=Lu_t$, $L=\Delta-x\cdot\nabla$, while $\nabla P_tf=e^{-t}P_t\nabla f$. Invariance $\int P_tg\,d\gamma_d=\int g\,d\gamma_d$ follows because $e^{-t}X+\sqrt{1-e^{-2t}}Y$ is standard Gaussian for independent standard $X,Y$. Differentiation is justified by [F2]; the integration-by-parts boundary terms vanish by bounded derivatives and Gaussian decay. [F1, F2, F3, given, algebra]

1.2 Put $v=\nabla u_t$, $H=D^2u_t$, $K=I(u_t)^2+|v|^2$ and $J(t)=\int\sqrt K\,d\gamma_d$. The identity $\nabla Lu=L\nabla u-\nabla u$, Gaussian integration by parts, and $II''=-1$ give $$J'(t)=\int\frac{-\|I'(u_t)vv^T-I(u_t)H\|_F^2+|Hv|^2-\|H\|_F^2|v|^2}{K^{3/2}}\,d\gamma_d\le0.$$ To verify the displayed computation, differentiating $J$ first gives $\int[II'Lu+v\cdot\nabla Lu]/\sqrt K$. Integrating both $Lu$ and each $Lv_i$ by parts leaves numerator $-I'^2|v|^4+2II'v^THv-I^2\|H\|_F^2-\|H\|_F^2|v|^2+|Hv|^2$, the displayed square expansion. Rowwise Cauchy–Schwarz gives $|Hv|^2\le\|H\|_F^2|v|^2$. All operations on compact time intervals are dominated because $I(u_t)$ has a fixed positive lower bound, derivatives are bounded, and Gaussian polynomial moments are finite. [F2, F3, step 1.1, algebra]

2.1 As $t\to\infty$, $u_t(x)\to\int f\,d\gamma_d$ and $|\nabla u_t|\le e^{-t}\|\nabla f\|_\infty\to0$. Dominated convergence and step 1.2 yield $$I\left(\int f\,d\gamma_d\right)\le\int\sqrt{I(f)^2+|\nabla f|^2}\,d\gamma_d\le\int I(f)\,d\gamma_d+\int|\nabla f|\,d\gamma_d.$$ Replacing a smooth $[0,1]$-valued $f$ by $\eta+(1-2\eta)f$ and letting $\eta\downarrow0$ extends this inequality to smooth $[0,1]$-valued functions with bounded derivatives. [F2, step 1.1, step 1.2, algebra]

3.1 Let $D$ be a nonempty finite union of closed balls of one common positive radius. Its boundary is contained in finitely many spheres, which have Lebesgue and hence Gaussian measure zero. For $h>0$ put $f_h=(1-\operatorname{dist}(\cdot,D)/h)_+$. Distance is $1$-Lipschitz, since $\operatorname{dist}(x,D)\le|x-y|+\operatorname{dist}(y,D)$ and one may interchange $x,y$. Thus $0\le f_h\le1$ and it is $1/h$-Lipschitz. Outside finitely many inner and outer cutoff spheres and nearest-center bisector hyperplanes it is smooth, its gradient has norm at most $1/h$, and its gradient vanishes outside $(D+hB_2^d)\setminus D$. These exceptional sets have Lebesgue measure zero by Fubini in suitable orthogonal coordinates. [F1, F2, construct, algebra]

3.2 Convolve $f_h$ with the nonnegative bumps $\rho_\delta$ from [F5]. The convolutions are smooth, valued in $[0,1]$, have bounded derivatives, and converge uniformly to $f_h$. On almost every coordinate line the distance formula is a finite piecewise smooth minimum of distances to centers, so $f_h$ is absolutely continuous there with derivative bounded by $1/h$. One-dimensional integration by parts and Fubini show $\nabla(f_h*\rho_\delta)=(\nabla f_h)*\rho_\delta$. At each point off the exceptional hypersurfaces the latter converges to $\nabla f_h$, and its norm is at most $1/h$. Dominated convergence against Gaussian probability therefore passes step 2.1 to $f_h$ and gives $$I\left(\int f_h\,d\gamma_d\right)\le\int I(f_h)\,d\gamma_d+\frac{\gamma_d(D+hB_2^d)-\gamma_d(D)}h.$$ As $h\downarrow0$, $f_h\to\mathbf1_D$ and $I(f_h)\to0$, so $I(\gamma_d(D))$ is at most the lower right derivative of the neighborhood mass. [F2, F3, F5, step 2.1, step 3.1, algebra]

4.1 Set $D_t=D+tB_2^d$ and $V(t)=\gamma_d(D_t)$. On each bounded time interval $V$ is Lipschitz: for $h>0$, $V(t+h)-V(t)$ is bounded by the sum of masses of finitely many spherical shells. Gaussian density is bounded; the Euclidean volume of a shell of bounded radius is at most a constant times $h$, by polar coordinates or the volume formula for balls. Each $D_t$ is again a finite union of equal-radius balls, so step 3.2 gives $V'(t)\ge I(V(t))$ almost everywhere. On a compact time interval $0<V(t)<1$, since $D_t$ is nonempty with interior and bounded; hence $\Phi^{-1}\circ V$ is absolutely continuous there and has derivative $V'/I(V)\ge1$ almost everywhere. The fundamental theorem gives $$\gamma_d(D+rB_2^d)\ge\Phi(\Phi^{-1}(\gamma_d(D))+r).$$ [F1, F3, F6, step 3.2, algebra]

5.1 For nonempty compact $K$ and $r>0$, choose $0<\delta<r$ and cover $K$ by finitely many closed $\delta$-balls centered in $K$; call their union $D_\delta$. Then $K\subseteq D_\delta\subseteq K+\delta B_2^d$ and $D_\delta+(r-\delta)B_2^d\subseteq K+rB_2^d$. Step 4.1 gives $\gamma_d(K+rB_2^d)\ge\Phi(\Phi^{-1}(\gamma_d(K))+r-\delta)$; let $\delta\downarrow0$. For Borel $A$, inner regularity provides compact $K\subseteq A$ with mass arbitrarily close to $\gamma_d(A)$. Each $K+rB_2^d$ is compact and contained in $A+rB_2^d$, so taking the supremum gives the asserted inner-measure bound. If $\gamma_d(A)=0$ the right side is zero; if it is one, compact inner approximation gives lower bound one. At $r=0$, [F4] identifies the inner and ordinary measures of $A$. [F4, step 4.1, given, choose, algebra] ∎

## Source notes

The full Bobkov paper and the complete Chafaï–Lehec semigroup proof were read. The sharp functional inequality is proved by the local derivative computation above; the finite-ball cutoff and compact approximation supply the full neighborhood passage without an imported spherical isoperimetry, coarea theorem, or Rademacher theorem.

## Statement

Assume AC and countable choice. Let $\mu$ be a centered tight Borel Gaussian law on a real separable Banach
space $B$, with covariance RKHS $H$ and unit ball $H_1$. For every Borel set
$A\subseteq B$ and $r\ge0$,
$$\mu_*(A+rH_1)\ge \Phi\!\left(\Phi^{-1}(\mu(A))+r\right),$$
where $\mu_*(S)=\sup\{\mu(K):K\subseteq S,\ K\text{ compact}\}$ is the inner
measure and $\Phi^{-1}(0)=-\infty$, $\Phi^{-1}(1)=+\infty$. When
$A+rH_1$ is Borel, its inner measure equals its ordinary $\mu$-measure.

## Facts & Assumptions


[A1] AC and countable choice are assumed by the finite-dimensional Gaussian and countable-cylinder interfaces ([[def-axiom-of-choice]], [[def-countable-choice]]).

[A2] Under AC, the real dominated-extension theorem supplies HB for the Hahn–Banach dual-norming interface ([[thm-hahn-banach-dominated-extension]], [[def-hahn-banach-extension-principle-relative]]).

[F1] For Borel $E\subseteq\mathbb R^d$ and $r\ge0$, Gaussian inner measure satisfies
$\gamma_{d,*}(E+rB_2^d)\ge\Phi(\Phi^{-1}(\gamma_d(E))+r)$
([[thm-finite-dimensional-gaussian-isoperimetric-expansion]]). This supplier proves the sharp finite-dimensional expansion locally.

[F2] The covariance RKHS $H$ is a Hilbert space continuously and injectively embedded in $B$, with $\ell(ih)=\langle h,[\ell]\rangle_H$
([[def-banach-gaussian-covariance-operator-and-rkhs]], [[thm-banach-gaussian-covariance-rkhs-is-well-defined]]).

[F3] The Hilbert unit ball $H_1$ is compact in the Banach norm
([[lem-banach-gaussian-rkhs-unit-ball-is-compact]]).

[F4] Borel probabilities on Polish spaces are inner regular
([[thm-borel-probability-measures-on-polish-spaces-are-inner-regular]]).

[F5] A separable metric space has a countable base, and countable choice selects one cover member for each relevant basis element ([[def-separable-space]], [[def-countable-choice]]).

[F6] Probability is continuous from above on decreasing measurable sets
([[thm-continuity-from-above-for-measures]]).

[F7] Under HB, distinct points in a normed space are separated by a continuous linear functional ([[cor-relative-hahn-banach-dual-norming]]).

## Proof


**Given:** AC, countable choice, a centered tight Borel Gaussian law $\mu$ on a real separable Banach space $B$, its covariance RKHS $H$, and $H_1=\{h\in H:\|h\|_H\le1\}$.

1.1 First let $F=T^{-1}(M)$ be a closed finite-coordinate cylinder, with $T=(\ell_1,\ldots,\ell_k):B\to\mathbb R^k$ continuous and $M$ closed. Let $Q=\operatorname{span}\{[\ell_i]:1\le i\le k\}\subset H$, choose an orthonormal basis $e_1,\ldots,e_m$, and choose representatives $\varphi_j\in B^*$ for $e_j$. Set $G=\sum_{j=1}^m\varphi_j(W)e_j$ and $S=T\circ i|_Q$. The vector of coefficients is standard Gaussian on $Q$ because its covariance matrix is the identity. For each $i$, $[\ell_i]=\sum_j\langle[\ell_i],e_j\rangle_H e_j$; by the covariance quotient and [F2], the residual $\ell_i(W)-\ell_i(iG)$ has variance $\|[\ell_i]-\sum_j\langle[\ell_i],e_j\rangle_H e_j\|_H^2=0$. Hence $T(W)=S(G)$ almost surely. The map $S$ is injective: if $S(q)=0$, then $\langle q,[\ell_i]\rangle_H=0$ for every $i$, and these classes span $Q$, so $q=0$. [F2, given, choose]

1.2 Now let $A\subseteq B$ be Borel with $0<\mu(A)<1$, and fix $\beta<\Phi^{-1}(\mu(A))$. By [F4] choose compact $K\subseteq A$ with $\mu(K)>\Phi(\beta)$. For each $x\notin K$ and $y\in K$, [F7] gives $\ell_y\in B^*$ with $\ell_y(x)\ne\ell_y(y)$. The open sets $U_y=\{z:|\ell_y(z)-\ell_y(y)|<|\ell_y(x)-\ell_y(y)|/3\}$ cover $K$; compactness gives a finite subcover $U_{y_1},\ldots,U_{y_q}$. For every $z\in K$, some $i$ has $z\in U_{y_i}$, which forces $\ell_{y_i}(z)\ne\ell_{y_i}(x)$. Thus the finite coordinate map $T_x=(\ell_{y_1},\ldots,\ell_{y_q})$ satisfies $T_x(x)\notin T_x(K)$. The cylinder $F_x=T_x^{-1}(T_x(K))$ is closed, contains $K$, and excludes $x$, since $T_x(K)$ is compact. The open complements $B\setminus F_x$ cover $B\setminus K$. By [F5] this cover has a countable subcover: for every basis element meeting $B\setminus K$ and contained in a cover member, countable choice selects one such member; every point is covered by one selected member. If the subcover is finite, repeat one member to index it by $j\ge1$. [A1, A2, F4, F5, F7, given, choose]

2.1 If $m=0$, then $T(W)=0$ almost surely, so $\mu(F)$ is zero or one; the endpoint convention, $0\in H_1$, and inner regularity [F4] give the claimed inequality. If $m>0$, define $E=S^{-1}(M)\subset Q$. It is closed and $\mu(F)=\gamma_Q(E)$. For $r\ge0$, $E_r=E+r(Q\cap H_1)$ is closed because its second summand is compact. Thus [F4] identifies its inner and ordinary Gaussian measures, and [F1] gives $\gamma_Q(E_r)\ge\Phi(\Phi^{-1}(\gamma_Q(E))+r)$. Let $C_r=T^{-1}(S(E_r))$, a closed finite-coordinate cylinder because $S$ is a linear isomorphism from finite-dimensional $Q$ onto the closed subspace $S(Q)$; injectivity of $S$ and $T(W)=S(G)$ give $\mu(C_r)=\gamma_Q(E_r)$. If $y\in C_r$, write $T(y)=S(u+v)$ with $u\in E$ and $v\in r(Q\cap H_1)$. Then $T(y-i(v))=S(u)\in M$, so $y-i(v)\in F$ and $y\in F+rH_1$. Hence $C_r\subseteq F+rH_1$, and inner regularity [F4] gives $\mu_*(F+rH_1)\ge\mu(C_r)\ge\Phi(\Phi^{-1}(\mu(F))+r)$. [A1, F1, F2, F4, step 1.1, algebra]

3.1 Let $G_n=\bigcap_{j\le n}F_{x_j}$ for the countable subcover in step 1.2. Each $G_n$ is a closed finite-coordinate cylinder because it is a finite intersection of such cylinders; the sequence decreases, $\bigcap_nG_n=K$, and $\mu(G_n)\ge\mu(K)>\Phi(\beta)$. Applying step 2.1 yields $\mu_*(G_n+rH_1)\ge\Phi(\beta+r)$. The set $G_n+rH_1$ is closed: if $a_j+h_j$ converges with $a_j\in G_n$ and $h_j\in rH_1$, compactness [F3] gives a convergent subsequence of $h_j$, after which closedness of $G_n$ gives a limit representation. Thus [F4] gives equality of its inner and ordinary measures. [F3, F4, step 2.1, step 1.2]

4.1 The closed sets $G_n+rH_1$ decrease and their intersection is $K+rH_1$. Indeed, if $x=a_n+h_n$ with $a_n\in G_n$ and $h_n\in rH_1$ for every $n$, compactness [F3] gives a subsequence $h_{n_j}\to h\in rH_1$; then $a_{n_j}\to x-h$, and for each fixed $N$ the tail belongs to the closed set $G_N$, so $x-h\in K$. The reverse inclusion is immediate. Continuity from above [F6] gives $\mu(K+rH_1)\ge\Phi(\beta+r)$. Since $K\subseteq A$, $\mu_*(A+rH_1)\ge\Phi(\beta+r)$. Letting $\beta\uparrow\Phi^{-1}(\mu(A))$ proves the interior-probability case. If $\mu(A)=0$ the right side is zero; if $\mu(A)=1$, inner regularity [F4] and $0\in H_1$ give $\mu_*(A+rH_1)=1$. [F3, F4, F6, step 3.1, algebra] ∎

## Statement

Assume AC and countable choice. Let $\mu$ be a centered tight Borel Gaussian
law on a real separable Banach
space $B$, with covariance RKHS $H$, and let $w_0\in\overline H^{\,B}$.
Suppose $n\ge1$, $\varepsilon>0$, $C>1$,
$e^{-Cn\varepsilon^2}<1/2$, and
$\phi_{w_0}(\varepsilon)\le n\varepsilon^2$, where $\phi_{w_0}$ is the
concentration function. Then there is a measurable set $B_n\subseteq B$
such that
$$\log N(3\varepsilon,B_n,\|\cdot\|_B)\le6Cn\varepsilon^2,\qquad \mu(B\setminus B_n)\le e^{-Cn\varepsilon^2},$$
and
$$\mu\{\|W-w_0\|_B<2\varepsilon\}\ge e^{-n\varepsilon^2}.$$
These are prior-mass and sieve bounds only; they assert no posterior
contraction without separate statistical-distance and Kullback–Leibler
comparisons.

## Facts & Assumptions

[A1] AC and countable choice are inherited from the Gaussian translation and Banach expansion suppliers ([[def-axiom-of-choice]], [[def-countable-choice]]).

[A2] Under AC, the real dominated-extension theorem supplies the Hahn–Banach principle HB used by the dual-norming interface ([[thm-hahn-banach-dominated-extension]], [[def-hahn-banach-extension-principle-relative]]).

[F1] The concentration function satisfies
$\phi_{w_0}(\varepsilon)=
\inf_{\|h-w_0\|_B<\varepsilon}
\{\|h\|_H^2-\log\mu(\varepsilon B^\circ)\}$
([[def-gaussian-prior-concentration-function]]).

[F2] For $h\in H$, the law of $W+h$ has density
$\exp(z_h-\|h\|_H^2/2)$ with respect to $\mu$
([[thm-cameron-martin-translation-for-separable-banach-gaussian-law]]).

[F3] The Gaussian expansion inequality gives
$\mu_*(A+rH_1)\ge\Phi(\Phi^{-1}(\mu(A))+r)$
for Borel $A$ ([[thm-borell-sudakov-tsirelson-expansion-for-banach-gaussian-law]]).

[F4] $H_1$ is compact in the Banach norm
([[lem-banach-gaussian-rkhs-unit-ball-is-compact]]).

[F5] A standard normal has density
$(2\pi)^{-1/2}e^{-z^2/2}$
([[def-standard-normal-and-normal-laws]]).

[F6] A Borel subset of a Polish space is inner regular, so its inner measure
equals its probability
([[thm-borel-probability-measures-on-polish-spaces-are-inner-regular]]).

[F7] The joint law of $(W,z_h)$ is determined by its norming coordinates and $z_h$; its finite centered Gaussian coordinate laws are invariant under simultaneous negation ([[lem-separable-banach-has-countable-norming-family]], [[lem-countable-norming-family-determines-borel-laws]], [[def-multivariate-normal-law]], [[thm-cameron-martin-translation-for-separable-banach-gaussian-law]]).

## Proof


**Given:** $\mu,B,H,w_0,n,\varepsilon,C$ as in the Statement. Set $t=n\varepsilon^2$ and $p=\mu(\varepsilon B^\circ)$.

1.1 The hypothesis [F1] implies $p\ge e^{-t}>0$, because every candidate $h$ has $\|h\|_H^2\ge0$. Fix $h\in H$. Take a countable norming family for $B$ and append the scalar coordinate $z_h$; this is a countable norming family for $B\times\mathbb R$ with the maximum product norm. By [F7], each finite coordinate vector is centered Gaussian and hence invariant under negation, so countable law determination makes the joint law symmetric under $(x,z)\mapsto(-x,-z)$. Thus, since $\varepsilon B^\circ$ is symmetric, $\int_{\varepsilon B^\circ}e^{-z_h(x)}\,d\mu(x) =\int_{\varepsilon B^\circ}\cosh(z_h(x))\,d\mu(x) \ge p.$ The Cameron–Martin identity [F2] for $-h$ now gives $\mu(h+\varepsilon B^\circ)\ge e^{-\|h\|_H^2/2}p$. [A1, A2, F1, F2, F7, given, algebra]

2.1 For each $\delta>0$, choose $h\in H$ with $\|h-w_0\|_B<\varepsilon$ and $\|h\|_H^2-\log p<\phi_{w_0}(\varepsilon)+\delta\le t+\delta$. Since $\|h\|_H^2/2-\log p\le\|h\|_H^2-\log p<t+\delta$, and $h+\varepsilon B^\circ\subset w_0+2\varepsilon B^\circ$, step 1.1 gives $\mu\{\|W-w_0\|_B<2\varepsilon\}\ge e^{-t-\delta}$. Letting $\delta\downarrow0$ proves the small-ball lower bound. [F1, step 1.1, choose, algebra]

2.2 Let $b=\Phi^{-1}(e^{-Ct})<0$ and $M=-2b>0$, and set $B_n=\varepsilon B^\circ+MH_1$. This is open, hence measurable. Since $p\ge e^{-t}$ and $C>1$, monotonicity of $\Phi^{-1}$ gives $\Phi^{-1}(p)>b$. By [F3], $\mu(B_n)\ge \Phi(\Phi^{-1}(p)+M) >\Phi(-b)=1-e^{-Ct}.$ The set $B_n$ is open and therefore Borel, so [F6] identifies its inner measure with $\mu(B_n)$. Thus $\mu(B\setminus B_n)\le e^{-Ct}$. [F3, F6, step 1.1, algebra]

2.3 Choose a maximal finite set $\{h_1,\ldots,h_N\}\subset MH_1$ with pairwise distances greater than $2\varepsilon$; such a set exists and covers $MH_1$ by closed $2\varepsilon$-balls because $MH_1$ is compact by [F4]. The open balls $h_i+\varepsilon B^\circ$ are disjoint. Step 1.1 and $\|h_i\|_H\le M$ imply each has $\mu$-measure at least $e^{-M^2/2}p$. Hence $N e^{-M^2/2}p\le1$ and $\log N\le M^2/2-\log p\le M^2/2+t$. Every point of $B_n$ lies within $3\varepsilon$ of one of the $h_i$, so $N(3\varepsilon,B_n,\|\cdot\|_B)\le N$. [F1, F2, F4, step 1.1, construct]

3.1 Completing the square in the standard normal density [F5] gives $E e^{-\lambda Z}=e^{\lambda^2/2}$. For $x\ge0$, on $\{Z\le-x\}$ one has $e^{-xZ}\ge e^{x^2}$, so $\Phi(-x)=P(Z\le-x)\le e^{-x^2}E e^{-xZ}=e^{-x^2/2}$. With $x=\sqrt{2Ct}$ this gives $\Phi(-\sqrt{2Ct})\le e^{-Ct}=\Phi(b)$, hence $-\sqrt{2Ct}\le b<0$ and $b^2\le2Ct$. Consequently $\log N(3\varepsilon,B_n,\|\cdot\|_B)\le2b^2+t\le4Ct+t\le5Ct\le6Ct$, using $C>1$. Step 2.2 supplies the complement bound and step 2.1 the small-ball bound. No posterior statement follows from these three prior inequalities alone. [F5, step 2.1, step 2.2, step 2.3, algebra] ∎

## Statement

Let $W$ be a centered Gaussian random element in a real normed space $B$. Let $\ell\in B^*$ satisfy $\operatorname{Var}(\ell(W))=\tau^2>0$, and let $\mathbb H$ be a Hilbert subspace of $B$ with nonnegative squared norm. For $w_0\in B$, define
$$\phi_{w_0}(\epsilon)=\inf_{\substack{h\in\mathbb H\\\|h-w_0\|_B<\epsilon}}\left\{\|h\|_{\mathbb H}^2\right\}-\log\Pr(\|W\|_B<\epsilon),$$
with $\inf\varnothing=+\infty$. Then for every $\epsilon>0$,
$$\phi_{w_0}(\epsilon)\ge \log(1/\epsilon)-C_\ell,\qquad C_\ell=\log\!\left(\frac{2\|\ell\|_{B^*}}{\sqrt{2\pi}\tau}\right).$$

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** A centered Gaussian random element, a continuous linear functional with positive variance, and the displayed nonnegative RKHS approximation penalty.

[F1] [[def-standard-normal-and-normal-laws]]: a centered scalar Gaussian with variance $\tau^2>0$ has density bounded above by $(\sqrt{2\pi}\tau)^{-1}$.

[F2] [[thm-logarithm-derivative-and-integral]]: $\log y=\int_1^y dt/t$ for $y>0$.

## Proof




1.1 On the event $\{\|W\|_B<\epsilon\}$, continuity and linearity give $|\ell(W)|\le\|\ell\|_{B^*}\|W\|_B<\|\ell\|_{B^*}\epsilon$. The interval $(-\|\ell\|\epsilon,\|\ell\|\epsilon)$ has length $2\|\ell\|\epsilon$, so its scalar Gaussian probability is at most its length times the density bound in [F1]. Therefore $\Pr(\|W\|_B<\epsilon)\le\frac{2\|\ell\|_{B^*}}{\sqrt{2\pi}\tau}\epsilon.$ [F1, given, algebra]

2.1 The approximation penalty in the displayed definition is nonnegative. Taking negative logarithms of the bound in step 1.1 and adding this penalty yields $\phi_{w_0}(\epsilon)\ge\log(1/\epsilon)-\log(2\|\ell\|_{B^*}/(\sqrt{2\pi}\tau))$, which is the asserted constant. [F2, step 1.1, given, algebra] ∎

## Source notes

The source defines the Gaussian concentration function as an RKHS approximation cost plus centered small-ball exponent. The one-dimensional projection bound is proved here and does not use a source inequality.

## Statement

Let $\epsilon_n>0$ satisfy $\epsilon_n\to0$ and $n\epsilon_n^2\to\infty$. For the centered tight Gaussian prior in each branch, let $\mu$ be its law and let $B$ be a separable closed Banach carrier with the norm inherited from that branch's stated function space, as supplied by [[lem-tight-borel-gaussian-law-has-separable-support]]. Write $\mathbb H$ for the covariance RKHS of $\mu$ on $B$, and define
$$\phi_{w_0}(\epsilon)=\inf_{\substack{h\in\mathbb H\\\|h-w_0\|_B<\epsilon}}\left\{\|h\|_{\mathbb H}^2-\log\mu(\epsilon B^\circ)\right\},\qquad \epsilon B^\circ=\{u\in B:\|u\|_B<\epsilon\}.$$
Suppose $\phi_{w_0}(\epsilon_n)\le n\epsilon_n^2$.

In each branch, parameter-to-data densities are jointly measurable and the posterior $\Pi_n$ is the data-indexed normalization of the prior times the likelihood on fibers with finite positive evidence.

1. **Log-Gaussian density estimation.** On a measurable space $(\mathsf X,\mathcal A)$ with sigma-finite measure $\nu$, let $W$ be a tight centered Borel Gaussian random element in $\ell^\infty(\mathsf X)$, and let $w_0$ belong to its support. Assume path evaluation $(w,x)\mapsto w(x)$ is jointly measurable, $Z_w=\int e^w\,d\nu\in(0,\infty)$ for prior-almost every $w$ and for $w_0$, and set $p_w=e^w/Z_w$, $p_0=p_{w_0}$. For IID data $X_1,\ldots,X_n\sim P_0$, sufficiently large fixed $M$ gives
$$E_0\Pi_n\{w:h(P_w,P_0)>M\epsilon_n\mid X^n\}\longrightarrow0.$$
When $0<\nu(\mathsf X)<\infty$, bounded paths imply the required normalizers are finite and positive.

2. **Binary regression.** Let $(X_i,Y_i)$ be IID, with $X_i\sim G$, $Y_i\in\{0,1\}$ and $P_0(Y=1\mid X=x)=f_0(x)=\Psi(w_0(x))\in(0,1)$. Assume $\Psi:\mathbb R\to(0,1)$ is differentiable, $\sup|\Psi'|<\infty$, and $\sup|\Psi'/[\Psi(1-\Psi)]|<\infty$. Suppose the prior is either a tight centered Gaussian law in $L^2(G)$ with a jointly measurable evaluation version representing its $L^2(G)$ element almost everywhere, or a tight centered Gaussian law in $\ell^\infty(\mathsf X)$ with jointly measurable evaluation and bounded $w_0$; in either case $w_0$ belongs to the prior support. Then for sufficiently large fixed $M$,
$$E_0\Pi_n\{\|\Psi(w)-f_0\|_{L^2(G)}>M\epsilon_n\mid (X_i,Y_i)_{i=1}^n\}\longrightarrow0.$$

3. **Fixed-design Gaussian regression.** For deterministic $x_1,\ldots,x_n$, assume independent $Y_i\sim N(w_0(x_i),\sigma_0^2)$, a centered tight Borel Gaussian prior $W$ in $\ell^\infty(\mathsf X)$ with $w_0$ in support, and an independent prior on the standard deviation $\sigma$ supported on a fixed $[a,b]\subset(0,\infty)$ containing $\sigma_0$, with Lebesgue density bounded below by a positive constant. Put $\rho_n=\max\{\epsilon_n,\sqrt{\log n/n}\}$ for $n\ge2$. Then for sufficiently large fixed $M$,
$$E_0\Pi_n\{\|w-w_0\|_n+|\sigma-\sigma_0|>M\rho_n\mid Y_{1:n}\}\longrightarrow0.$$
The sharper conclusion with $\epsilon_n$ in place of $\rho_n$ holds if the Gaussian law is not the point mass at zero. It also holds when $W=0$ almost surely and the scale-prior density is bounded above on a neighborhood of $\sigma_0$; this extra upper bound is needed only for that sharper degenerate-prior alternative, not for the universal $\rho_n$ conclusion. In the nondegenerate case $\rho_n=O(\epsilon_n)$, so the two formulations differ only by the fixed constant $M$. Here $\|w-w_0\|_n^2=n^{-1}\sum_i(w(x_i)-w_0(x_i))^2$.

The concentration-function hypothesis is interpreted on a separable Banach space carrying the prior. For a tight Gaussian law initially given in nonseparable $\ell^\infty(\mathsf X)$, the separable-support reduction is [[lem-tight-borel-gaussian-law-has-separable-support]]; the norm and prior law are restricted to that support space.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The three model contracts above, a common rate sequence satisfying $\epsilon_n\to0$ and $n\epsilon_n^2\to\infty$, and the displayed Gaussian concentration-function inequality.

[F8] [[thm-support-of-banach-gaussian-is-closure-of-rkhs]]: under AC and countable choice, a centered tight Borel Gaussian law on a real separable Banach space has support equal to the Banach-norm closure of its covariance RKHS.

[F9] [[def-gaussian-prior-concentration-function]]: the current definition uses $\inf_{\|h-w_0\|_B<\epsilon}\{\|h\|_{\mathbb H}^2-\log\mu(\epsilon B^\circ)\}$ for $w_0\in\overline{\mathbb H}^{\,B}$.

[F10] [[thm-gaussian-concentration-sieve-bounds]]: under AC and countable choice, the full-squared concentration hypothesis supplies measurable sieves with $\log N(3r,B_n,\|\cdot\|_B)\le6Cnr^2$, prior tail at most $e^{-Cnr^2}$, and mass at least $e^{-nr^2}$ in the $2r$-ball about the truth. Its sharp finite-dimensional expansion and Banach expansion suppliers have local proofs.

[F11] [[def-borel-gaussian-random-element-on-a-separable-banach-space]]: a centered Borel Gaussian random element is a Borel-measurable map into a real separable Banach space whose continuous linear images are centered normal.

[F12] [[def-banach-gaussian-covariance-operator-and-rkhs]]: under AC, the covariance RKHS is the completed covariance-form quotient embedded as a Hilbert space of shifts in the Banach space.

[A2] In the fixed-design branch the scale prior has density at least $c>0$ on $[a,b]$. For $r\downarrow0$, including when $\sigma_0$ is an endpoint, its $r$-neighborhood therefore has prior mass at least $cr$ once $r<b-a$. An upper density bound is assumed only in the sharper degenerate-prior alternative stated above.

[A3] Assume AC and countable choice for the Gaussian concentration-sieve interface [[def-axiom-of-choice]], [[def-countable-choice]]. The separate Hahn–Banach extension principle used in [F5] is not inferred from these assumptions.

[A4] Assume the separate relative Hahn–Banach extension principle [[def-hahn-banach-extension-principle-relative]] for the separable-support reduction [F5]; it is not silently deduced from AC.

[F1] [[lem-iid-posterior-denominator-lower-bound-from-kl-mass]]: for a jointly measurable dominated IID model, local prior mass at least $e^{-Cn\delta_n^2}$ on a set with directional KL and log-square at most $\delta_n^2$ gives a denominator lower bound $e^{-(C+2)n\delta_n^2}$ except with probability at most $(n\delta_n^2)^{-1}$.

[F2] [[lem-iid-sieve-entropy-produces-exponential-tests]]: same-metric packing entropy at radius $\delta_n$ bounded by $n\delta_n^2$ gives tests with exponentially small null and uniform alternative errors outside a sufficiently large multiple of $\delta_n$; for density $L^2$ the densities must be uniformly bounded.

[F3] [[lem-log-gaussian-density-supnorm-controls-local-likelihood-distances]], [[lem-binary-regression-l2-controls-local-likelihood-distances]], and [[lem-fixed-design-gaussian-regression-controls-local-likelihood-distances]] give the local Hellinger, density-$L^2$, directional KL and log-square comparisons used on this page.

[F4] [[lem-independent-observation-posterior-denominator-lower-bound]] and [[lem-independent-posterior-splitting-from-tests-and-sieve-tail]] give the non-IID denominator bound and the tested-numerator/sieve-tail split used in the IID and fixed-design arguments.

[F5] [[lem-tight-borel-gaussian-law-has-separable-support]]: a tight Borel Gaussian law in a Banach space is carried by a separable closed subspace without changing its support or inherited norm.

[F6] [[thm-tonelli-theorem-for-sigma-finite-product-spaces]]: joint measurability and Tonelli make the log-Gaussian normalizer a measurable function of the path.

[F7] [[lem-nondegenerate-gaussian-small-ball-controls-log-radius]]: if the prior has a nonzero Gaussian direction, $\phi_{w_0}(\epsilon)\le n\epsilon^2$ implies $\log(1/\epsilon)\le n\epsilon^2+C$ for a fixed constant.

[F13] A separable Banach space has a countable norming family under the declared Hahn–Banach and countable-choice assumptions. Thus a centered Gaussian law different from $\delta_0$ has a continuous linear functional with positive variance. [[lem-separable-banach-has-countable-norming-family]].


[F14] A supremum-norm sieve with covering entropy at radius $3r_n$ bounded by $6Cnr_n^2$ supplies fixed-design Gaussian tests outside a sufficiently large empirical-mean-plus-scale ball, with arbitrarily prescribed fixed exponential error exponent. [[lem-fixed-design-gaussian-regression-exponential-tests]].

[F15] The centered Gaussian residual-energy statistic has an exponential tail at deviations of order $R/\sqrt n$ for fixed $R$. [[lem-gaussian-linear-and-quadratic-statistic-tail]].

## Proof

**Given:** The hypotheses of the Statement and its three distinct model branches.

1.1 The separable-support reduction [F5] leaves the inherited norm, law and support point unchanged. For the first two branches use the rate $r_n=\epsilon_n$; for the universal fixed-design branch use $r_n=\rho_n$. The concentration function is nonincreasing in its radius, because its feasible RKHS approximation set grows and centered small-ball probabilities increase. Thus $\phi_{w_0}(r_n)\le\phi_{w_0}(\epsilon_n)\le n\epsilon_n^2\le nr_n^2$. Both choices satisfy $r_n\to0$ and $nr_n^2\to\infty$. By [F8], the support point lies in the RKHS closure. [A3, A4, F5, F8, F9, F11, F12, given, algebra]

1.2 In log-Gaussian density estimation, evaluation measurability and Tonelli [F6] make $w\mapsto Z_w$ measurable. On its full-prior positive-finite set, $(w,x)\mapsto e^{w(x)}/Z_w$ is a jointly measurable density family. The $2r_n$ supremum ball has directional KL at most $2e^{4r_n}r_n^2$ and log-square at most $16r_n^2$ by [F3]. Choose a fixed sufficiently large $k$. Its prior mass is at least $e^{-nr_n^2}$ by [F10], so [F1] at radius $kr_n$ gives a denominator at least $e^{-A nr_n^2}$ for fixed $A=1+2k^2$ except with probability tending to zero. [F1, F3, F6, F10, step 1.1, given, choose]

1.3 In binary regression, [F3] places the $2r_n$ prior ball in a directional KL/log-square set of radius $k^2r_n^2$ for a fixed sufficiently large $k$. Its mass is at least $e^{-nr_n^2}$ by [F10], so [F1] gives the same type of denominator bound. The joint Bernoulli densities relative to $G\otimes\#$ are bounded by one, as required for the density-$L^2$ tests in [F2]. [F1, F2, F3, F10, step 1.1, given, choose]

1.4 For the universal fixed-design branch take $r_n=\rho_n$. On $\|w-w_0\|_\infty<2r_n$ and $|\sigma-\sigma_0|<r_n$, [F3] bounds average directional KL and log-square by $Kr_n^2$ for fixed $K$. Independence and [A2], together with [F10], give joint local prior mass at least $cr_ne^{-nr_n^2}$. Since $r_n\ge\sqrt{\log n/n}$, eventually $\log(1/r_n)\le\tfrac12\log n\le\tfrac12nr_n^2$; hence this mass is at least $e^{-C_0nr_n^2}$ for fixed $C_0$. The independent-observation denominator lemma in [F4] applies. [A2, F3, F4, F10, step 1.1, given, algebra]

2.1 For each branch choose $C>1$ larger than its denominator exponent; eventually $e^{-Cnr_n^2}<1/2$. Apply the prior sieve theorem [F10] using step 1.1 to get measurable $B_n$ with entropy at radius $3r_n$ at most $6Cnr_n^2$ and tail at most $e^{-Cnr_n^2}$. The same theorem supplies the local prior mass used in steps 1.2–1.4. [A3, F8, F9, F10, step 1.1, given, choose]

3.1 In the density branch intersect $B_n$ with the measurable positive-finite-normalizer set, changing its prior tail by zero. From a radius-$3r_n$ cover, select a valid center for every cover ball meeting that intersection; finite selection doubles the radius to $6r_n$ without increasing the number. The pairwise norm comparison [F3] sends this to a Hellinger cover of radius at most $7r_n$ for large $n$. Thus any $14r_n$-separated set has size at most $e^{6Cnr_n^2}$. Taking packing radius at least $\max\{14,\sqrt{6C}\}r_n$, [F2] gives tests with null and uniform sieve alternative errors at most $e^{-Tnr_n^2}$ for any fixed desired $T>A$, by increasing the alternative multiple. The denominator and sieve tail now satisfy the posterior split in [F4], proving contraction in probability. [F2, F3, F4, F6, F10, step 1.2, step 2.1, given, choose]

3.2 In binary regression the norm-ball and sieve cover map by [F3] to density-$L^2$ balls and covers of constant times $r_n$. Taking packing radius at least twice the cover radius and at least $\sqrt{6C}r_n$ gives packing entropy at most its squared radius times $n$. By [F2] and [F4], the tests, denominator and sieve tail prove contraction in probability. Since the joint Bernoulli densities satisfy $d_2(q_w,q_{w_0})=\sqrt2\|\Psi(w)-f_0\|_{L^2(G)}$, this is the stated binary distance. [F2, F3, F4, F10, step 1.3, step 2.1, choose, algebra]

3.3 In fixed-design regression take the product sieve $B_n\times[a,b]$. Its prior tail is at most $e^{-Cnr_n^2}$, and its function component has the radius-$3r_n$ cover from step 2.1. The local fixed-design testing lemma [F14] gives tests outside $\|w-w_0\|_n+|\sigma-\sigma_0|>Mr_n$ with errors at most $e^{-Tnr_n^2}$ for any fixed $T$ by choosing fixed $M$ large. Choose $T$ and $C$ above the denominator exponent in step 1.4. The posterior split [F4] proves the universal $\rho_n$ contraction in probability. [F4, F10, F14, step 1.4, step 2.1, given, choose]

4.1 If the Gaussian law is not $\delta_0$, [F13] supplies a continuous linear functional with nonzero Gaussian variance. Indeed, otherwise every member of a countable norming family would vanish almost surely, forcing $\|W\|=0$ almost surely. By [F7] there is a fixed constant $D$ such that $\log(1/\epsilon_n)\le n\epsilon_n^2+D$. Put $t_n=n\epsilon_n^2\to\infty$; then $\log n=\log t_n+2\log(1/\epsilon_n)\le3t_n+2D$ eventually, since $\log t_n\le t_n$. Consequently $\rho_n\le C_1\epsilon_n$ for fixed $C_1$. The universal conclusion in step 3.3 therefore proves the sharper $\epsilon_n$ conclusion after enlarging $M$ by $C_1$. [A3, A4, F7, F13, step 3.3, given, algebra]

4.2 Now suppose $W=0$ almost surely and its scale density $g$ is bounded above by $U<\infty$ on $|\sigma-\sigma_0|<\delta$ within $[a,b]$. The support assumption forces $w_0=0$. Put $S_n=\sum_iY_i^2$, $q=S_n/(n\sigma_0^2)$, and $L_n(\sigma)=(\sigma_0/\sigma)^n\exp[(1-\sigma_0^2/\sigma^2)S_n/(2\sigma_0^2)]$. On $E_R=\{|S_n-n\sigma_0^2|\le R\sqrt n\}$, write $z=(\sigma-\sigma_0)/\sigma_0$. Compactness of the positive scale interval and Taylor's formula give constants $c,C>0$ independent of $n,R$ with $$-Cn(\sigma-\sigma_0)^2-CR\sqrt n|\sigma-\sigma_0|\le\log L_n(\sigma)\le-cn(\sigma-\sigma_0)^2+CR\sqrt n|\sigma-\sigma_0|.$$ For verification, its deterministic part is $n[-\log(1+z)+(1-(1+z)^{-2})/2]$, negative away from zero, with second derivative $-2$ at zero; the remaining term is $(S_n-n\sigma_0^2)(1-(1+z)^{-2})/(2\sigma_0^2)$, bounded by $CR\sqrt n|z|$. The residual-energy tail in [F15] with zero mean shift gives $\limsup_nP_0(E_R^c)\le2e^{-c_0R^2}$ for fixed $R$. [F3, F15, given, algebra]

4.3 On $E_R$ integrate the likelihood over $|\sigma-\sigma_0|\le1/\sqrt n$ within $[a,b]$. This interval has length at least $1/\sqrt n$ for large $n$, even at an endpoint; [A2] and step 4.2 bound its integral below by $c_R/\sqrt n$ for some $c_R>0$. On the local neighborhood where $g\le U$, substitute $u=\sqrt n(\sigma-\sigma_0)$ in the numerator outside $M\epsilon_n$. Dividing by that lower bound gives at most $C_R\int_{|u|>M\sqrt n\epsilon_n}e^{-cu^2+CR|u|}du\to0$, since $n\epsilon_n^2\to\infty$. Outside the local neighborhood, step 4.2 bounds $L_n$ by $e^{-c'n}$ for large $n$, whose integral against the entire probability prior is at most $e^{-c'n}$; after dividing by the denominator this also tends to zero. First let $n\to\infty$ and then $R\to\infty$. This proves the sharper degenerate-prior contraction in probability for every fixed $M>0$. [A2, step 4.2, given, algebra]

5.1 In each proved branch the posterior tail is a random variable $T_n\in[0,1]$ converging to zero in probability. For $\eta>0$, $ET_n\le\eta+P(T_n>\eta)$; first take the limit superior and then $\eta\downarrow0$. Thus all asserted expectation limits follow. The universal fixed-design rate requires no upper bound on the scale density; the sharper degenerate alternative uses only the explicitly local upper bound. [step 3.1, step 3.2, step 3.3, step 4.1, step 4.3, given, algebra] ∎

## Remarks

A scale density bounded below supplies interval mass of order its radius, but the Gaussian concentration condition does not bound the logarithm of that radius when $W=0$. An unrestricted scale density can have spikes that make the originally proposed arbitrary $\epsilon_n$ rate false; [[cex-degenerate-gaussian-scale-prior-can-break-arbitrary-concentration-rate]] gives an explicit counterexample. The universal $\rho_n$ rate retains every allowed prior. A nonzero Gaussian direction or a local upper scale-density bound in the degenerate case supplies the sharper alternative by separate proved arguments.

## Statement

On $[0,1]$ with Lebesgue measure, take $W(x)=Z$ for all $x$, where $Z\sim N(0,1)$, and let the truth be $w_0=0$. The normalized log-Gaussian density prior is exactly the point mass at the uniform density. The concentration condition holds at $\epsilon_n=\sqrt{\log n/n}$ for all sufficiently large n.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The constant process $W(x)=Z$, standard normal $Z$, and uniform truth $p_0=1$.

[F1] [[def-standard-normal-and-normal-laws]]: the standard normal has density $\varphi(z)=e^{-z^2/2}/\sqrt{2\pi}$, which is bounded below on $[-1,1]$ by $\varphi(1)>0$.

[F2] [[thm-gaussian-process-posterior-contraction]]: in the log-Gaussian branch, a verified concentration condition and the model hypotheses imply expected posterior contraction in Hellinger distance.

## Verification

1.1 Every prior path is constant, so $Z_W=\int_0^1 e^Zdx=e^Z$ and $p_W(x)=1=p_0(x)$. Thus the posterior distribution of the density itself is the point mass at $p_0$ for every data vector; its posterior mass outside every positive Hellinger ball is exactly zero. [given, algebra]

1.2 The RKHS approximation term at $w_0=0$ is zero because the zero vector belongs to every Hilbert space. For $0<\epsilon\le1$, [F1] gives $\Pr(\|W\|_\infty<\epsilon)=\Pr(|Z|<\epsilon)\ge2\varphi(1)\epsilon$, hence $\phi_0(\epsilon)\le-\log(2\varphi(1)\epsilon)$. For $\epsilon_n=\sqrt{\log n/n}$, $n\epsilon_n^2=\log n$ and $-\log\epsilon_n\le\frac12\log n$ for large n, so $\phi_0(\epsilon_n)\le n\epsilon_n^2$ eventually. [F1, given, algebra]

2.1 The density family is jointly measurable and all normalizers are positive and finite. Step 1.2 verifies the concentration premise; applying the log-Gaussian branch of [F2] gives the stated rate, while step 1.1 gives the stronger exact posterior conclusion. [F2, step 1.1, step 1.2] ∎

## Statement

Take repeated design point $x_0$, prior $W(x)=Z\sim N(0,1)$, truth $w_0=0$, true standard deviation $\sigma_0=1$, and an independent prior $\sigma\sim\operatorname{Unif}[1/2,3/2]$. For $\epsilon_n=2\sqrt{\log n/n}$, the GP concentration and scale-local-mass conditions hold for all sufficiently large n.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The stated constant Gaussian prior, fixed design, truth and independent uniform scale prior.

[F1] [[def-standard-normal-and-normal-laws]]: the standard-normal density is bounded below by $\varphi(1)>0$ on $[-1,1]$.

[F2] [[thm-gaussian-process-posterior-contraction]]: under its fixed-design conditions, with $\rho_n=\max\{\epsilon_n,\sqrt{\log n/n}\}$ for every allowed prior and with the sharper $\epsilon_n$ rate for a nonzero Gaussian law, expected posterior mass outside a sufficiently large empirical-L²-plus-scale ball tends to zero.

## Verification

1.1 The support of $W$ is the line of constant functions, which contains $w_0$. The RKHS approximation cost at zero is zero, and $\|W\|_\infty=|Z|$. For $\epsilon\le1$, [F1] gives $\Pr(\|W\|_\infty<\epsilon)\ge2\varphi(1)\epsilon$, so $\phi_0(\epsilon)\le-\log(2\varphi(1)\epsilon)$. [F1, given, algebra]

1.2 At $\epsilon_n=2\sqrt{\log n/n}$, $n\epsilon_n^2=4\log n$ while $-\log(2\varphi(1)\epsilon_n)=\frac12\log n-\frac12\log\log n+O(1)$, so the concentration inequality holds for large n. Also, for $\epsilon_n<1/2$, the uniform scale prior assigns mass $2\epsilon_n$ to $(1-\epsilon_n,1+\epsilon_n)$; its negative log is $O(\log n)=O(n\epsilon_n^2)$. [F1, given, algebra]

2.1 The scale prior is independent and has density one, the true scale lies in the interior of its fixed positive interval, and every design point is $x_0$. Steps 1.1–1.2 verify the concentration and scale-local-mass checks, so the sharper fixed-design conclusion follows from [F2]: this Gaussian law is nonzero and the stated rate already satisfies $\rho_n=\epsilon_n$. [F2, step 1.1, step 1.2] ∎

## Statement

Let the covariate space contain one point $x_0$, let $G=\delta_{x_0}$, and take $W(x_0)=Z\sim N(0,1)$. With the logistic link $\Psi(u)=(1+e^{-u})^{-1}$ and truth $w_0(x_0)=0$, the hypotheses of the binary-regression branch hold at $\epsilon_n=\sqrt{\log n/n}$ for all sufficiently large n.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The one-point covariate law, logistic link, constant Gaussian prior and true response probability $f_0(x_0)=1/2$.

[F1] [[def-standard-normal-and-normal-laws]]: $Z$ has density $\varphi(z)=e^{-z^2/2}/\sqrt{2\pi}$ and positive mass on every interval around zero.

[F2] [[thm-gaussian-process-posterior-contraction]]: under its binary-regression hypotheses, expected posterior mass outside a sufficiently large $L^2(G)$ ball tends to zero.

## Verification

1.1 Differentiation gives $\Psi'(u)=\Psi(u)(1-\Psi(u))$, so $|\Psi'(u)|\le1/4$ and $|\Psi'(u)/[\Psi(u)(1-\Psi(u))]|=1$. The true response probability is $\Psi(0)=1/2\in(0,1)$, and $w_0=0$ is in the support of the scalar standard-normal prior. [given, algebra]

1.2 Here $L^2(G)$ is isometric to $\mathbb R$ and $\|W\|_{L^2(G)}=|Z|$. The RKHS approximation cost at zero is zero. By [F1], for $0<\epsilon\le1$, $\Pr(|Z|<\epsilon)\ge2\varphi(1)\epsilon$, so $\phi_0(\epsilon_n)\le-\log(2\varphi(1)\epsilon_n)$. With $\epsilon_n=\sqrt{\log n/n}$, this is at most $n\epsilon_n^2=\log n$ for all sufficiently large n. [F1, given, algebra]

2.1 The joint Bernoulli density relative to $G\otimes\#$ is bounded by one, and the constant-process evaluation is jointly measurable. Steps 1.1–1.2 verify the remaining link, truth-support and concentration conditions; applying the binary-regression branch of [F2] yields expected posterior contraction in $L^2(G)$. [F2, step 1.1, step 1.2] ∎

## Statement

Let $W\equiv0$, $w_0=0$, and let its covariance RKHS be $\mathbb H=\{0\}$. Define $\phi_0(\epsilon)=\inf_{h\in\mathbb H,\,|h-w_0|<\epsilon}\{\|h\|_{\mathbb H}^2\}-\log\Pr(|W|<\epsilon)$. For $n$ large, set $\epsilon_n=\sqrt{\log\log n/n}$ and take an independent $\sigma\sim\operatorname{Unif}[1/2,3/2]$ with true value $\sigma_0=1$. Then $\phi_0(\epsilon_n)=0$, $\epsilon_n\to0$, and $n\epsilon_n^2\to\infty$, but
$$-\log\Pr(|\sigma-\sigma_0|<\epsilon_n)\not=O(n\epsilon_n^2).$$
Thus the Gaussian concentration condition alone does not verify the joint local prior-mass bound used by the denominator argument for the unknown-scale branch. This calculation is a proof-gap example, not a posterior counterexample.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The point-mass Gaussian prior, the displayed rate sequence, and the independent uniform scale prior.

[F1] [[thm-logarithm-derivative-and-integral]]: $\log x=\int_1^x dt/t$ and, for $x\ge1$, $\log x\le2\sqrt{x}$.

## Verification

1.1 The RKHS of the point-mass prior is $\{0\}$; its approximation cost at $w_0=0$ is zero. Also $\Pr(|W|<\epsilon)=1$ for every $\epsilon>0$, so the explicitly defined concentration function satisfies $\phi_0(\epsilon)=0$. [given, algebra]

1.2 For $n$ sufficiently large, $\epsilon_n<1/2$, hence the uniform prior assigns mass $2\epsilon_n$ to $(1-\epsilon_n,1+\epsilon_n)$. Therefore $-\log(2\epsilon_n)=\tfrac12\log n-\tfrac12\log\log\log n-\log2,$ while $n\epsilon_n^2=\log\log n$. Along $n_m=\lceil e^{e^m}\rceil$, the first quantity grows on the order of $e^m$ and the second on the order of $m$, so their ratio is unbounded. [given, algebra]

2.1 Since $\log\log n\to\infty$ and $\log\log n/n\to0$, the rate has $n\epsilon_n^2\to\infty$ and $\epsilon_n\to0$ while the scale interval mass has negative logarithm not $O(n\epsilon_n^2)$ by step 1.2. Thus the Gaussian concentration condition does not establish this particular denominator-mass check; it does not establish failure of posterior contraction. A locally bounded scale density, as in this uniform example, admits a separate parametric contraction argument. [F1, step 1.2, given] ∎

## Statement refuted

For every centered tight Gaussian prior, including $W=0$, a Gaussian concentration condition $\phi_0(\epsilon_n)\le n\epsilon_n^2$, $\epsilon_n\to0$ and $n\epsilon_n^2\to\infty$, together with an independent scale prior on a fixed positive compact interval having density bounded below, would imply expected posterior contraction at a sufficiently large fixed multiple of $\epsilon_n$ in fixed-design Gaussian regression. The following counterexample concerns that unrestricted rate claim, not the universal logarithmic-floor or sharper qualified alternatives proved on the A page.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** AC; $W=w_0=0$; independent data $Y_i\sim N(0,1)$; scale parameter $\sigma\in[1/2,3/2]$; and the explicit prior below.

[F1] A normal $N(0,\sigma^2)$ has Lebesgue density $(2\pi\sigma^2)^{-1/2}e^{-y^2/(2\sigma^2)}$. [[def-standard-normal-and-normal-laws]].

[F2] A nonnegative measurable density defines a measure and nonnegative weighted sums of measures are measures. [[def-measure-with-density]], [[thm-nonnegative-weighted-sums-of-measures]].

[F3] A geometric series with ratio in $(0,1)$ converges. [[thm-geometric-series]].

[F4] The centered Gaussian residual-energy bound implies $P(|\sum_{i=1}^nY_i^2-n|>R\sqrt n)\le2e^{-cR^2}$ whenever $R/\sqrt n$ is sufficiently small, for an absolute $c>0$. [[lem-gaussian-linear-and-quadratic-statistic-tail]].

[A1] AC is assumed for the normal-law interface. [[def-axiom-of-choice]].

## Counterexample

**Given:** The model above. Fix $k_0=4$, put $\delta_k=e^{-k!}$ and $I_k=[1+\delta_k,1+\delta_k+\delta_k^4]$ for $k\ge k_0$, and let $U_J$ denote the uniform law on an interval $J$ of positive length.

1.1 The intervals $I_k$ are disjoint subsets of $[1/2,3/2]$, since $\delta_{k+1}=\delta_k^{k+1}$ and $\delta_{k+1}+\delta_{k+1}^4<\delta_k$. The series $S=\sum_{k\ge k_0}\sqrt{\delta_k}$ is positive and finite, bounded by $\sum_{k\ge k_0}e^{-k/2}$ using $k!\ge k$ and [F3]. Define $$\Pi_\sigma=\tfrac12U_{[1/2,3/2]}+\sum_{k\ge k_0}m_kU_{I_k},\qquad m_k=\frac{\sqrt{\delta_k}}{2S}.$$ By [F2] this is a probability measure with a measurable Lebesgue density bounded below by $1/2$ on the required interval. Its spike densities need not be bounded above near $1$. [F2, F3, given, construct, algebra]

1.2 The zero Gaussian law is tight and centered, with support $\{0\}$, covariance RKHS $\{0\}$ and $\phi_0(\epsilon)=0$ for every positive $\epsilon$. For all sufficiently large $n$ define $\epsilon_n=\sqrt{\log\log\log n/n}$, choosing arbitrary positive initial terms. Then $\epsilon_n\to0$, $n\epsilon_n^2\to\infty$ and the concentration condition holds. Put $n_k=\lceil k^4\delta_k^{-2}\rceil$. Since $\log n_k=2k!+O(\log k)$, $\log\log\log n_k=O(\log k)$ and tends to infinity; hence $\epsilon_{n_k}/\delta_k=O(\sqrt{\log k}/k^2)\to0$. [given, construct, algebra]

2.1 Put $S_n=\sum_iY_i^2$. By [F1] the likelihood ratio relative to true scale $1$ is $$L_n(\sigma)=\exp\{-n\log\sigma+(1-\sigma^{-2})S_n/2\}.$$ On $E_k=\{|S_{n_k}-n_k|\le k\sqrt{n_k}\}$, [F4] gives $P_0(E_k^c)\to0$. Write $q=S_{n_k}/n_k$. Maximizing the log likelihood over all positive $\sigma$ gives its maximum $n_k(q-1-\log q)/2$ at $\sigma^2=q$. Since $|q-1|\le k/\sqrt{n_k}$, Taylor's formula gives $\sup_{\sigma\in[1/2,3/2]}L_{n_k}(\sigma)\le e^{Ck^2}$ for a constant independent of $k$. [A1, F1, F4, step 1.2, given, algebra]

2.2 Uniformly on $I_k$, $|\sigma-1|\le2\delta_k$. The function $d(\sigma)=-\log\sigma+(1-\sigma^{-2})/2$ satisfies $d(1)=d'(1)=0$ and has bounded second derivative near $1$, while $|1-\sigma^{-2}|\le C|\sigma-1|$. On $E_k$ this gives $$\log L_{n_k}(\sigma)\ge-Cn_k\delta_k^2-Ck\sqrt{n_k}\delta_k\ge-C'k^4.$$ Thus the posterior denominator is at least $m_ke^{-C'k^4}$ on $E_k$. [F1, step 1.1, step 1.2, step 2.1, algebra]

3.1 Fix $M>0$. Since $\epsilon_{n_k}/\delta_k\to0$, the set $J_k=\{|\sigma-1|\le M\epsilon_{n_k}\}$ misses $I_k$ and all earlier spikes for large $k$. Its prior mass is at most $M\epsilon_{n_k}+\sum_{j>k}m_j$. The later sum is $O(\sqrt{\delta_{k+1}})$: successive square-root terms have ratio at most $1/2$ for $k\ge k_0$, so [F3] bounds the tail by twice its first term. Steps 2.1–2.2 therefore give $$\Pi_\sigma(J_k\mid Y^{n_k})\le e^{Ck^2+C'k^4}\frac{M\epsilon_{n_k}+O(\sqrt{\delta_{k+1}})}{m_k}.$$ Both terms tend to zero: $\epsilon_{n_k}/\sqrt{\delta_k}=O(e^{-k!/2}\sqrt{\log k}/k^2)$ and $\sqrt{\delta_{k+1}/\delta_k}=e^{-kk!/2}$ dominate the polynomial exponent. [F3, step 1.1, step 1.2, step 2.1, step 2.2, algebra]

4.1 On events with probability tending to one, step 3.1 makes posterior mass within $M\epsilon_{n_k}$ tend to zero for every fixed $M$. Thus its expected mass outside that radius tends to one, by boundedness and $P_0(E_k^c)\to0$. The mean function is identically its truth, so this is exactly failure for the combined empirical-mean-plus-scale distance. All original scale-prior and Gaussian concentration assumptions are satisfied, refuting the unrestricted rate claim. [step 1.1, step 1.2, step 2.1, step 3.1, algebra] ∎
